title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) that embeds a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pipeline. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks), gpt-5-mini as generator, and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator as ground truth, the executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one generated candidate per pair evaluated under both arms). Observed outcomes: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify → optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); no verifier rejections occurred and no repairs were invoked. Paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). Crucially, the preregistered minimum detectable effect calculations assumed independent per‑arm sampling; because execution_contract.independent_condition_generation was set to false, the executed run tests the verifier’s marginal effect conditional on identical generated candidates. We release full preregistration and execution artifacts and provide a minimal, artifact‑anchored recipe to test the original estimand under independent sampling (change execution_contract.independent_condition_generation to true; increase allowed model calls to permit one independent generation per arm per task; optionally increase repair budget and set nonzero temperature). All provenance, raw responses, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes are archived for deterministic reproduction (preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0; master prompt provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba; execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b07e1ffabb163657f56ae893fd65fc12d5307ea1ff3bb98f7cf43329a).

sections.introduction: LLM‑assisted intent→configuration automation promises operational gains but raises reliability and safety concerns because autoregressive generation is stochastic and can produce syntactically plausible yet unsafe device commands. A common operational architecture to constrain this risk is Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR): (1) generate candidate configuration(s); (2) deterministically verify correctness/safety with a verifier oracle; (3) if rejected, invoke a bounded repair loop that uses verifier diagnostics to guide subsequent generation attempts. This paper reports a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored empirical test of the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic formal verifier into an LLM pipeline. Research question (preregistered): Does embedding a formal verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM GVR loop increase detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improve bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation? We executed the frozen plan (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) and publish the complete provenance and artifacts so readers can deterministically verify every reported number.
sections.related_work: Work motivating generate→verify architectures and bounded repair has appeared across regulated code generation, RAG/Tool‑augmented LLM agents, and intent‑based NetOps. Representative leads used in the preregistration and literature verification include: (i) Generate‑Verify‑Repair (GVR) architectural framing for deterministic control over stochastic generation [R. Cadenas, Convergent Correctness; doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899], and (ii) formal network verification frameworks suitable as deterministic oracles (e.g., weighted NetKAT decision procedures for quantitative properties; doi:10.1145/3808318). Survey and systems work on LLMs for intent‑based configuration and RAG‑anchored agentic NetOps provide context but do not replace the need for preregistered controlled studies with full execution provenance (see OpenAlex entries W4414359351, W4400072049, W4386722061). Our contribution is not a new verifier or generator; it is an artifact‑anchored empirical test with frozen design, deterministic logging, and released cryptographic artifact manifests.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan: The preregistered plan (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) fixed estimands, sampling plan, generation/repair budgets, retry policy, and stopping rules before running (preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (the within‑task difference in proportion of verifier rejections/accepts). Design: paired within‑task, Npairs=270 (3 vendor styles × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks). Validation subset: 20% stratified holdout (54 tasks) for verifier↔emulator concordance checks. Generator and verifier: declared generator gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) called via the recorded provider openai_responses; deterministic network verifier executed against Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator used as emulator ground truth. Execution contract decisive fields (frozen and archived): execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false (shared_initial_candidate semantics), initial_generation_calls_per_task=1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1, planned_episode_count=540. Scoring: each candidate validated deterministically by deterministic_netops_validator_v5; per‑episode JSONs include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, validator decision, and detailed validator_trace (paths and SHA‑256s recorded under execution/scoring/*.json). Statistical plan: primary test = paired binary comparison (exact McNemar two‑sided), paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed=1729). Failure policy: model/API call failures allowed up to two retries (exponential backoff); retries and any infrastructure failures are logged in execution/execution_log.jsonl; no retries were needed in this run. All raw responses, provider call traces, scoring JSONs, and the full per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest are archived (see execution/*).
sections.results: Execution and primary counts (artifact‑anchored). Planned episodes: 540 (270 paired tasks). Completed: 540; failed: 0. Model calls used: 270 (one shared generation per pair because independent_condition_generation=false). Aggregated scoring: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded accepted 270/270 (100%). Contingency table (artifact analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 62cd99d7bf35cab7ee751f4faae9004784597d06684b884750e66083a3e52f21): n11=270, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Statistical inference: paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; bootstrap_seed = 1729). Repair activity: zero verifier rejections occurred in the guarded arm; bounded repair was not invoked. Verifier↔emulator concordance on validation subset (54 tasks): 54/54 agreement (false_accept=0; false_reject=0) as recorded in per‑episode scoring JSONs. Representative artifacts (examples): preregistration JSON SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0; master prompt archive provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba; execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b07e1ffabb163657f56ae893fd65fc12d5307ea1ff3bb98f7cf43329a; execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 350bfaa2eec0deb0e16121f5e7effa2d8743d28f3f014856107acfabbb42d87e (contains validator_trace for a representative episode). Interpretation of quantitative outcomes. The degenerate CI and p‑value arise from zero discordant pairs (n10=n01=0). Those inferential quantities therefore reflect the observed contingency under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics; they do not imply that verifiers are generally ineffective. The executed run is a conditional test: it measures verifier insertion effect conditional on identical generated candidates per paired task.
sections.discussion: Why the run produced a provenance‑backed null. Two preregistered design choices produced the observed contingency: (A) execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) caused a single generated candidate per task to be evaluated in both arms; (B) with the chosen generator/prompt/settings (gpt-5-mini as declared in execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...), every generated candidate in the suite satisfied the deterministic verifier rule set. These facts are recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json and in every per‑episode scoring JSON. Consequence for the estimand and power. The preregistered power and minimum detectable effect calculations assumed independent per‑arm sampling. Because the executed run used shared candidate semantics, the planned MDE does not apply to the observed contingency. The observed p=1.0 and CI=[0.00,0.00] are arithmetic consequences of zero discordant pairs and must be interpreted as conditional on identical candidates. Operational implications. The run identifies a concrete evaluation regime where an LLM generator (as configured) produces verifier‑acceptable outputs for the chosen synthetic task bank; in that regime inserting a deterministic verifier (with the deployed rule set and a bounded repair budget of 1) will not change accept/reject counts under shared candidate evaluation. This is a useful boundary condition for operational architects: when a generator reliably produces verifier‑acceptable candidates, the marginal observed effect of a verifier (under shared candidate semantics) will be zero. Reproducible minimal follow‑up recipe (artifact‑anchored) to test the original preregistered estimand: change only the following preregistered fields (paths and keys appear in execution/execution_manifest.json and the preregistration): (1) set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation = true so each arm receives an independent stochastic generation; (2) set execution_contract.maximum_model_calls >= 540 (one independent generation per arm per task) and ensure model_calls_used budget permits 540 generator calls; (3) in execution/model_configuration.json set temperature to a nonzero value (or provide a per‑call seed list) to expose sampling variability; (4) optionally increase execution_contract.maximum_repair_calls_per_task > 1 to study bounded repair convergence. After applying these minimal, artifact‑recorded changes, re‑run the archived harness to test the original estimand with independent per‑arm sampling; all file paths and field names required to make these edits are present in the released artifacts. Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared candidate choice removed between‑arm stochasticity and thus altered the estimand the power calculation targeted; this is a design (not execution) mismatch and is fully logged. Construct validity: the synthetic tasks encode operationally meaningful patterns (shutdown→change→restore; make‑before‑break), but they do not substitute for full production heterogeneity. External validity: single model and single verifier rule set were used; results do not generalize to all generators, cameras, or production devices. Conclusion validity: the zero‑discordant counts preclude informative hypothesis rejection for the original independent‑sampling estimand and make the original power calculation inapplicable; this fact is recorded in analysis artifacts and the deterministic reconciliation manifest.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired study that integrates a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline and released the complete provenance bundle. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and the chosen generator/settings, the single generated candidate per task was verifier‑acceptable for all N=270 tasks so the verifier/repair path was not invoked; the observed paired difference is 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.0). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: generation semantics (shared candidate vs independent sampling) critically determine whether a verifier insertion is testable under a preregistered paired estimand. We publish the exact artifacts and a minimal reproducible recipe to enable deterministic follow‑ups that test the original estimand with independent per‑arm sampling. All execution, scoring, and analysis artifacts are archived and hashed for deterministic reproduction (see execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/*).

limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to complex, noisy, adversarial, or production NetOps environments; emulator behavior can differ from heterogeneous production devices.
Single‑model evaluation: only a single generator (gpt-5-mini) was used; no claim of multi‑model generality should be inferred.

Generation semantics constraint: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per task and thereby eliminated between‑arm stochastic sampling variance; the preregistered MDE calculations assumed independent sampling and are therefore inapplicable to the observed contingency.

Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1); multi‑attempt repair strategies were not evaluated and could change outcomes.

Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: a single deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and rule set were used; different verifier conservatism or policy choices will change false‑accept/reject tradeoffs.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator‑validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on production devices or multi‑vendor deployments.
